REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are citizens of Nigeria and Mexico.1 They are appealing a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 26, 2021, rejecting their refugee protection claim.2 Ms. XXXX is the designated representative of the Minor Associate Appellants.3

[2] With respect to Mexico, Mr. XXXX alleges that he is unable to return there because he participated in a demonstration against the collaboration of corrupt government officials with drug cartel members, particularly the Sinaloa Cartel (SC), in order to kidnap and kill 46 students. Both he and the Associate Appellant allegedly fear that the SC would kill them or their children as retribution because he was participating in that demonstration and seeking to submit a complaint with Mexican police authorities.4 In XXXX 2016, they left Mexico back to Nigeria.5

[3] With respect to Nigeria, Mr. XXXX alleges that he fears arrest and detention by the Nigerian police for his identity as a bi-sexual man, after his romantic partner confessed that he was involved in a same-sex relationship with the Principal Appellant.6 Mrs. XXXX alleges that she fears returning to Nigeria because she fears that police authorities will harass, extort her, or even imprison her if she does not hand over her husband and that she fears for her children's safety in Nigeria.7 They arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and filed their refugee protection claim on January 15, 2020.8

[4] During the hearing, the RPD focused on the following issues: credibility, state protection in Mexico, an IFA in Merida and nexus in Mexico.9 However in its decision, the RPD identified credibility as the determinative issue,10 and decided that the Principal Appellant has not established his sexual orientation as a bi-sexual male.11 The panel also underscored that it considered the IRB Chairperson's Guideline 9: Proceedings before the IRB involving Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression and Sex Characteristics (thereafter SOGIE Guideline), and which I note, has been updated after the RPD rendered its decision.12 The RPD determined that he did not have a well-founded fear of persecution with respect to his first country of citizenship Nigeria. and that consequently, he is not wanted by Nigerian authorities in relation to his sexual orientation.13 Consequently, the panel did not consider it necessary to decide on the credibility of his allegations with respect to his second country of citizenship Mexico.14

[5] On appeal, Mr. XXXX alleges that the RPD erred in its conclusion. This is because he submits that the RPD breached his right to procedural fairness;15 adopted a microscopic and over-zealous approach to his oral and written testimony; and did not meaningfully engage with all of the evidence with respect to the central issue of his claim, namely that he is bi-sexual.16 He also alleges that the RPD conducted its assessment of his testimony and the evidence without considering and applying the SOGIE Guidelines.17

[6] On February 11, 2022, I reached out to the Appellants to inform them that the RAD has identified a new issue in this appeal, namely the availability of an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) for the Appellants in Merida, Yucatan, and invited submissions from the Appellants should they have any. I also informed them that the RAD would be relying on the most recent version of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Mexico (September 2021). On February 25, 2022, the Principal Appellants made additional submissions with respect to the new issue.
DECISION

[7] I dismiss the appeal. For reasons different than those enumerated by the RPD, I find that the panel was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
[8] This is because I find that the Appellants have a viable IFA in Mérida, Yucatán if they return to Mexico.
BACKGROUND
Overview of the RPD decision

[9] In its decision, the panel enumerated the following reasons for rejecting the Appellants' refugee protection claim:
1. There were significant discrepancies between the Principal Appellant's written testimony and port of entry (PoE) notes, which undermined the credibility of his allegations that he was not involved in a same-sex relationship with a man named XXXX.18
2. The Appellant's response as to what a US-based immigration lawyer on the plane to Toronto advised him, namely that he should not say certain things to Canadian immigration officials, and why he did not share those instructions with his wife, was not persuasive. The RPD, therefore, concluded that he did not speak to a US-based immigration lawyer on the plane as alleged.19
3. The behavior of the Principal Appellant, who spoke on behalf of his family with the Canadian Border Service Agency (CBSA) officer upon arriving in Canada, and his delay in telling immigration officials of his alleged fear of persecution is inconsistent with someone who has a subjective fear.20 This, the panel found, undermined his overall credibility with respect to central allegations to his claim.21 The panel presented the following elements as justifications for this conclusion:
(a) In his first interview by a CBSA officer (XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019), the Appellant informed the officer that he was here on vacation and presented a return flight to Lagos, Nigeria for XXXX 2020 with British Airways.22
(b) Upon searching the phone of the Principal Appellant, he found a WhatsApp conversation with a person named XXXX XXXX XXXX allegedly based in Canada, indicating that the Appellants were searching for long-term rentals, and with her recommending that the Appellants purchase property, apply for a work permit and hide all documents and delete any incriminating messages before arriving in Canada.23
(c) When the CBSA officer concluded that the Appellants were not forthcoming about his purpose of travel to Canada and refused the Appellants' entry into Canada. At this point, the Principal Appellant chose to withdraw his application to enter Canada and to leave without delay.24 He then informed the CBCA officer that he and his family cannot return to Nigeria because their life is in danger and that they prefer to return to Mexico and purchased their tickets to Cancun, Mexico, for XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. They were then given entry for further examination that day.25 According to the RPD, the fact that he purchased tickets to Mexico, a country where he later alleged that he faces a risk of serious harm at the hands of the SC, undermines his allegation that he has a subjective fear of persecution.26
(d) In his written narrative attached to his BoC, the Principal Appellant indicated that he fears returning to Nigeria because Nigerian police seek to arrest him for being bisexual.27 However, after withdrawing his application to enter Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2019, according to the PoE notes on that day, the Principal Appellant then informs the CBSA officer that he feared a splinter group of Boko Haram,28 which he fears would kill his children.29
4. The evidence submitted by the Appellant does not overcome the credibility concerns that the panel had,30 most notably with respect to Mr. XXXX allegations that he is bisexual or a homosexual.31
NEW EVIDENCE

[10] The Appellants did not submit any new evidence to be considered under section 110(4) of the IRPA.32 Since there is no new evidence, in this case, I cannot hold an oral hearing as stipulated under section 110(6) of the IRPA.33
ANALYSIS

[11] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.34 I will not examine the correctness of the RPD's conclusion that the Principal Appellant is not credible with respect to his allegation that he fears persecution in Nigeria because of his sexual orientation as a bisexual man. This is because, after considering all of the evidence before me, I find that the Appellants, who allege harm by the SC, have a viable IFA in Mérida. Hence, I still find that the RPD was correct in its overall conclusion that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

[12] I based my assessment on the IFA two-prong test, namely that (1) there must be no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted in the part of the country identified as an IFA, in this case, Mérida, or that on a balance of probabilities, they would not be subjected personally to a danger of torture or a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment therein,35 and (2) that the conditions in the IFA of Mérida must be such that it would not be objectively unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellants for them to seek refuge there.36
The Principal Appellant's Allegations with respect to Mexico

[13] According to the PoE notes by the CBSA authorities, the Principal Appellant stated that he became a Mexican national after having a marriage of convenience with a Mexican national and that once he became a resident in Mexico, he sponsored his wife and son to join him.37 In his oral testimony, he testified that in 2008 he, his wife and his son, travelled to Mexico in 2008, and resided there until XXXX 2016.38 He also testified that he owned a XXXXbusiness there since 2012.39 In his written narrative, he also stated that "[w]e lived in relative peace in Mexico for approximately eight years before trouble made us return to Nigeria in XXXX 2016".40

[14] In his oral testimony, the Principal Appellant alleged that he fears the SC because it "comes to where we live and collect money from us steady and they always tell us that, "If you don't pay, we will kill you.41 On XXXX 2016, the Principal Appellant joined some students to demonstrate against the rumoured collaboration of corrupt government officials with powerful drug cartels to kidnap and kill people who were opposing their activities and their policies. He also alleges that the SC kidnapped 46 students, including a member of the Nigerian community in XXXX XXXX (where they resided).42Consequently, he and others went to report the issue to the police and demand protection, but those police authorities refused to take down their statement.43

[15] The Appellants decide to relocate to Mexico City for safety. Three days later, the SC allegedly visited the home of Mr. XXXX, a friend who had also participated in the protests and relocated to Mexico City after the events. The Principal Appellant alleges that the SC shot his friend in the presence of his family. According to the Associate Appellant, Mr. XXXX wife told her that the killers allegedly threatened that they would kill anyone who stands in their way or protests against them.44 During his testimony, the Principal Appellant alleged that the killers said that they would kill anyone who dares report them again to the police and that anyone who has tried to report them needs to leave Mexico within 14 days or be killed. The Appellants left Mexico in XXXX 2016.45
1. First Prong: Is there a possibility of persecution or likelihood of harm for the Appellants in the proposed IFA of Mérida?

[16] In determining whether or not the Appellants would be personally subjected to a risk of harm in Merida, I have assessed whether the alleged agents of harm, the SC, have the "the means" and motivation to locate them in those proposed IFA location46

[17] For the following reasons, I do not find that the Principal Appellant has established that the conditions of the first prong of the IFA test have been met. I reach this conclusion because I do not find that the alleged agent of harm, the SC has the motivation or the means to find and harm the Principal Appellant and his family in Mérida if he relocates there. Below are my reasons why.
A. The Alleged Means and Motivation of the SC to Find and Harm the Appellants in Mérida
(i) The Motivation

[18] During the RPD hearing, the panel asked the Principal Appellant to clarify, why he thought that the SC would, five years after leaving, still be motivated to find and harm him and his family if he relocates to Mérida. In response, the Principal Appellant testified that "the cartel, since we went to the police station, they are very upset about that so they don't want people confronting them or disobeying their order. So, and they are very upset. So even if I go to Mérida now and they have any -- like there they will still come to harm you."47 When the RPD then inquired how the Cartel would find out that he and his family returned to Mexico, he responded that "[s]o I can tell you now that the drug cartels, I can tell they are very powerful. They are very rich. They are connected to all the sort of government. So even I'm not --I know they even they even have our pictures because they get whatever they want because they're very powerful and they don't forget if you cross them. They don't forget."48

[19] Although I agree with the Principal Appellant that in principle, drug cartels such as the SC are rich and powerful, on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Principal Appellant has persuasively established that they would be motivated to find and harm him and his family because he reported the kidnapping of the students to the police and to do so many years after the incident allegedly took place.

[20] To begin with, I find that the Appellant's testimony was vague and lacked any significant details as to why the SC would be motivated to find him and his family in Mérida. When the RPD inquired a third time what the motivation would be of the SC to find them if they relocate to the proposed IFA location, he responded that "[s]o, these people, all the history, the knowledge we know about them, they don't ever forget. That's how they maintain their superiority, wherever they are. So, since the time we went to the police they were very upset and they say they are going to do something and they must do it whenever they have the pushing they will do it. So that was why we ran away from basically everybody."49 When the RPD then asked him how the SC would get the name of his wife and children, the Principal Appellant testified that "[t]hey are too powerful. Whatever they want they get. They work with the police. They work with every level of the government. They want you once they need anything. If they don't have it, they'll get it from the police."50

[21] I do not find that the Appellant has provided sufficient evidence to establish the credibility of these allegations. To begin with, at no point in time did the Principal Appellant allege that the SC sent threatening texts or made threatening calls to him or the other Appellants during their stay in Mexico. Nor did he allege that the SC have resorted to social media as a tool for extorting and threatening the Appellants with violence, as an article submitted by the Appellant suggests that drug cartels indicates that they sometimes do.51

[22] In addition, even if I were to presume that some police collaborate with the SC, because of widespread corruption, a phenomenon that is documented in the DNP,52 as the Principal Appellant testified, there is nothing on the record with police authorities that he submitted, or sought to submit, a complaint against the SC. This is because the Principal Appellant testified that the police refused to register the complaint that he sought to submit.53 This is reiterated by Counsel who mentions that when the Appellants sought to approach the Mexican Police to lodge a report, they were turned away.54 In the absence of any physical proof that the Principal Appellant did indeed seek to report the SC to the police (given that there was no physical police report accompanying personal information of the Appellants that may get stored along with it), I find that there is insufficient evidence that the SC would have the motivation to find his name or that of his wife and children in order to harm them, especially if they relocate to another part of Mexico such as Mérida.

[23] Moreover, I point to the testimony of the Principal Appellant and that of the Associate Appellant that the SC affiliated killers of Mr. XXXX threat was that they would pursue anyone who would report them to the police again or would protest against them again. At no point in time has the Principal Appellant alleged that he seeks to do either of these things in the future. Nor does my reading of the Appellants' testimony led me to understand that the SC threat implies or seeks retribution for the Principal Appellant's past involvement in the demonstration or reporting of SC activities to the police. Rather, I find that it implies, if credible, a warning to the Appellants that retribution will happen if they decide to demonstrate against them or report them once again to the police. Hence, I do not find that the Appellant has credibly and persuasively established that the SC would be motivated to find the Appellants because of a vendetta as alleged by Counsel in his further submissions,55 and by the Principal Appellant in his further submissions to the RAD.56

[24] Finally, I point out that as part of his personal evidence, the Appellant submitted an article from Wikipedia, entitled "2014-Iquala Mass Kidnapping".57 The article states that 43 students were abducted and disappeared in Iquala. The article also states that at least 80 suspects were arrested, including 44 police officers and that in June 2020, the leader of the United Warriors Cartel, Mr, Angel Casarrubias Salgadoalias was arrested and that he "is suspected of being responsible for the abductions and ordering of the murders of the abducted students."58 I find that the information in this article undermines the Appellant's allegations in his oral testimony that the SC was behind the abduction of the students,59 or that therefore, it would be motivated to find and harm the Appellants in the proposed IFA of Yucatán because they protested against this incident or sought to submit a complaint to police authorities in Iquala.

[25] In sum, and in light of the above, I find that the Principal Appellant's testimony and personal evidence fails to credibly establish that the agents of harm would, on a balance of probabilities, have the motivation to locate him and his family if he moved to the IFA of Mérida.
(ii) The Means

[26] During the RPD hearing, the Appellant alleged that once the SC "marks your name back, anywhere you are in Mexico they will get you."60 When the RPD asked the Principal Appellant to clarify how he knows that they would be able to find him anywhere in Mexico, he responded that "[o]kay, we're not the only people that they sought and caught. It's all over. Everybody know that they do that and also when we went to Mexico City, it was baffling on how they know immediately where Mr. XXXX (ph) was staying. Like the (inaudible) knowledge that they work with the police and also the military. So, they are very connected, well connected."61

[27] The Principal Appellant also alleged that they used a call tracker and that this is how they were able to identify the whereabouts of Mr. XXXX and track him down."62 When the RPD then inquired with the Appellant how he found out that the SC uses a tracker, he responded that somebody told him, but that he is unsure as to how it works.63 In his further submissions, the Principal Appellant alleges that a Response for Information Request (RIR) in the NDP on Mexico lends support to his allegations that drug cartels use a GPS tracker that they place on cars.64 During the RPD hearing, he also mentioned that somebody told him, but he does not know for sure that this is how they were able to find Mr. XXXX and kill him

[28] I do not find that the Principal Appellant has persuasively established that the SC would resort to a call tracker to identify the Appellant's whereabouts in Mérida many years after the initial incident took place. This is because the aforementioned RIR states that drug cartels in Mexico would be motivated to track someone outside of their areas if a large debt or a personal vendetta is motivating them to track someone outside their area of operation.65 Given that I have already found that there is insufficient evidence that there is a personal vendetta or large debt to motivate the SC to find and harm the Appellants in the IFA of Mérida, I find that the Appellant has not credibly established that the SC would use the GPS tracker against him and his family if they relocate to Mérida.

[29] Here, I also want to address the Appellant's allegations that they used 'a call tracker' to find and kill Mr. XXXX in Mexico City. In this regard, I want to underscore that one NDP source by the US Congressional Research Service contains a map which shows Mexico City falling within the area of influence of the SC.66 This, I find, explains why the SC was able to find and kill Mr. XXXX in Mexico City. It is also worth mentioning that another NDP source confirms that the SC operates in Mexico City and may even be growing in the capital.67 In other words, the objective documentary evidence lends support to the Appellant's allegation that the SC had the means to find his friend and maybe the Appellants themselves, had they stayed in Mexico City.

[30] By contrast, the same map indicates that the proposed IFA location of Mérida lies outside the area of influence of the SC,68 which supports my conclusion that the SC does not have the means to find and harm the Appellant if he relocates there with his family.

[31] When the RPD then informed the Principal Appellant that according to the objective country documentation, the SC does not have a presence in Mérida and asked him to clarify why he still thought they had the means to find and harm him there, he responded that they operate everywhere, including in Mérida, because the police will give them the information.69 In his further submissions, the Principal Appellant also alleges that the SC has vast resources and alliances that allows them to operate with impunity anywhere within Mexico and abroad and that they would use their affiliations with other cartels in the areas not under their primary control.70

[32] I do not agree with the Appellant that the objective documentary evidence supports his allegations that for the reasons he mentions, the SC would have the means to find and harm him and his family if they relocate to Mérida. While the SC may be a powerful cartel like the Appellant alleges, sources in the NDP, underscore that it is under a certain amount of pressure as of 2020. Thus, while some analysts in one source highlight that the SC remains powerful given its international dominance and its infiltration of the upper reaches of the Mexican government, other sources maintain that the SC is in decline, citing its breakup into factions and violence from inter and intra-organizational tensions. The source also states that the SC is facing violent competition from another cartel, the Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG), which split from the SC in 2010,71 and that the CJNG has battled against its former partner (the SC) in a number of regions and has emerged as Mexico's new most expansive cartel.72 Another source also underscores that the SC has been weakened by the infighting and power struggle.73

[33] In his further submissions to the RAD, the Principal Appellant pointed to a RIR of the NDP,74 to allege that the objective country documentation indicates that the SC operates in 17 states and has alliances with the Gulf Cartel, the Familia Michoacana and the Tijuana Cartel. However, my reading of the source does not support the Appellant's allegations. The RIR singled out by the Principal Appellant states that both the CJNG and the Gulf Cartel are enemies of the SC. It also states that the SC is in competition with the Juarez Cartel, and Los Zetas, and that the Tijuana Cartel might have resumed competition with the SC.75 In addition, while a RIR in the NDP does mention that the SC, the CJNG and the Gulf Cartel "may be present" in Yucatán or Mérida, it also underscores that "they "try to keep a low-profile" and there does not "seem" to be the establishment of a hegemony by any one organized crime group."76 This is because the State of Yucatán is not located among the drug routes or have an attractive market for drug dealing.77

[34] Given all of the above, I conclude that the Principal Appellant failed to establish that on a balance of probabilities, the agents of harm have the means to find the Appellants and harm them if they relocate to Mérida.
2. The Appellant's allegation that he would be persecuted in Mérida because he is a bisexual man

[35] In his oral testimony, the Principal Appellant alleges that living in Mexico would not be safe for him because he fears the SC and because he is bisexual.78 He also alleged that he did not expose his bisexual orientation, as he only had one friend, XXXX, who was also a Nigerian bisexual man. However, he also mentioned that they used to frequent gay bars and hang out.79 In Counsel's submissions to the RPD, he states that an IFA in Mérida is not viable for the Principal Appellant because he is a bisexual man who suppressed his sexual orientation while in Mexico and only maintained a secret fling with XXXX.80 In this regard, he also points out that the SOGIE Guidelines underscore that an IFA is not viable if an individual must conceal their sexual orientation in order to live in that location.81

[36] Furthermore, Counsel points out that the objective country documentation in the NDP on Mexico supports his allegations that in light of the particular circumstances for the Principal Appellant, the IFA of Mérida is neither safe nor reasonable. According to Counsel's written submissions to the RPD, and also to the Principal Appellant in his further submissions to the RAD, one RIR,82 underscores the following: that machismo is still embedded in Mexican culture which repercussions for homophobia and discrimination against sexual minorities; that changes in the legislative, judicial and health matters have changed the social situation very little; that more LGBT individuals were killed in 2017 and 2018 than in previous years and that there have been reported cases of violence and aggression by the police and of being detained for the LGBT status.83

[37] Similarly, he alleges that sources in another RIR,84 underscores there is an official recognition that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity continues to be a structural phenomenon with extensive social roots; that it has been promoted by the Catholic Church; that there is a lot of discrimination and violence towards the LGBTQ community in small cities and rural areas but that things have been improving in the last few years and that the areas where sexual minorities are most ostracized include Mérida.85 In his further submissions to the RAD, the Principal Appellant alleges that this RIR also indicates that the police subjects LGBTQ persons routinely to mistreatment while in custody.86

[38] I agree with the Appellant that individuals of diverse sexual orientations and/or gender identities, including bisexual men and women, clearly continue to experience discrimination and harassment in Mexico. I also agree with the Appellant that an IFA is not viable if an individual must conceal their sexual orientation in order to live in that location.

[39] However, for reasons I will explain below, I do not find that the Principal Appellant credibly established that the discrimination and harassment that he may face as a bisexual man if he relocates with his family to the IFA of Mérida, would rise to the level of persecution, or that the country conditions evidence support those allegations.

[40] The risk of a serious possibility of persecution must be assessed case by case while considering the degree of seriousness of the harm, its repetition and persistence, and whether the cumulative acts of discrimination amount to persecution. Discrimination may be considered persecution if it leads to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature for the claimant, for example, serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to enjoy privacy and family life, his right of access to public places, his right to move about freely or his right to education.87 However, discrimination does not always equate with persecution; since it may not always be serious enough to warrant being qualified as persecution.88 In determining the consequences of the alleged discrimination, I considered the personal circumstances of the Principal Appellant and his vulnerabilities.89 I also assessed the objective basis for his fear of persecution in order to determine if there is a foundation for it.

[41] I reviewed his claim to have a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of membership in a particular social group (bisexual men who are married and have a family) and concluded that on a balance of probabilities, there is no serious possibility that the Principal Appellant would be subjected to persecution in Mérida because of his bisexual orientation.90

[42] Firstly, with respect to the objective documentary evidence, I agree with the Principal Appellant that there is significant discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, motivated by social prejudice. I also agree that there are reports of violence and aggression against them and that sources indicate that there is a failure of police authorities to always investigate and punish those complicit in abuses. No doubt, these continue to be amongst the most significant human rights challenges facing LGBTQ individuals in Mexico, despite a gradual increase in public acceptance of them.91

[43] However, even though the rate at which changes take place to improve the situation of LGBTQ persons, guaranteed access to more rights has been slow, it is not true to say that progress on the ground is non-existent or minimal. In this regard, NDP-related sources underscore that important stridehave been made to further protect and uphold the rights of LGBTQ individuals in law, and in practice and to increase social acceptance of their fundamental nature. Here, I point to the Appellant's Memorandum of Appeal which acknowledges that while NDP sources state that there is a lot of discrimination and violence towards the LGBTQ community in small cities and rural areas, things have been improving in the last few years.

[44] To mention the legal progress that has taken place, one NDP-related source states that the first article of the Mexican constitution was updated to include discrimination based on sexual preference.92 Today, constitutionally regulated judicial mechanisms guarantee the rights of same-sex couples to marry, adopt, access social security, receive alimony, and enjoy family life. 93 In 2019, the Supreme Court ruled that a same-sex couple in one state should be allowed to register their child, to protect the best interest of the child and uphold principles of equality and non-discrimination. 94 Twelve Mexican states allow transgender people to change their names and gender markers on birth certificates through a simple administrative process before the state Civil Registry. In addition, 20 of the 32 Mexican states have legalized same-sex marriage.95

[45] Other sources also point out that since 2016, Mexico has been part of the LGBT Core Group of the United Nations and the Organization of American States. In 2017, it conducted a national survey on discrimination to better understand public perceptions of groups such as lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons. This resulted in the drafting of several important protocols that seek to ensure non-discriminatory access to health services and to foster a culture of respect for the human rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons in the health sector.96 Here, I also note that according to one source, migrants, asylum seekers and refugees can also receive medical treatment and HIV and sexually transmitted infection medication at no cost and regardless of immigration status.97 Organizations that work on promoting the rights of LGBTQ, such as JS14, have also recognized developments such as specific protocols, anti-discrimination campaigns, the National Day to Combat Homophobia, national surveys on non-discrimination and dialogues with social organizations for the protection of the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons.98 With respect to changing societal perceptions and efforts to combat misinformation, a source mentions that the National Commission to Prevent Discrimination wrote a letter condemning the Roman Catholic diocese of Mexicali for inciting homophobia by calling for anti-LGTBI protests.99

[46] Here, it is also worth mentioning that in correspondence with the Research Directorate, an activist and researcher who works on sexual and reproductive health and rights internationally and in Mexico and is affiliated with the Gay Latino Network, stated that the legislation to protect sexual minorities is only partially effective and that it is society itself which has been promoting change through campaigns, television shows and private companies that support the rights of LGBT persons.100 One other item in the NDP suggest that even though the shift is slow, societal perceptions are shifting. According to the 2014 National Catholic Opinion Survey by the Catholics for the Right to Decide, a non-profit organization that promotes sexual and reproductive rights, and Mexican consultancy agency (Research in Health and Demographics, based on the interview of 2,669 persons across Mexico who self-identified as Catholics, 87 percent of the Catholics surveyed indicated that they believe homosexuals and lesbians should have the same rights as everybody else, and 59 percent indicated that they support same-sex marriage.101

[47] Clearly, however, the objective country documentation also underscores those significant challenges continue to face efforts to realizing the ability of the LGBTQ community to access all of their rights equally and fully. And while I find that sources do reiterate that discriminatory practices and social misconceptions still persist against LGBTQ, I do not find that the information or statistics support the Principal Appellant's allegation that these practices amount cumulatively to persecution. In terms of access to work for example, according to the national study on LGBTI discrimination in the workplace by CEAV and Fundación Arcoiris, which was completed by 3,451 respondents across the country in 2018, an estimated 30 percent of respondents reported that being LGBTI was an obstacle to employment occasionally, 21 percent said frequently, and 10 percent said always, while 30 percent estimated that it was never an obstacle.102 Sources also state that the number of companies in Mexico that have adopted policies to promote LGBT equality and inclusion is increasing.103

[48] With respect to access to health, according to a 2018 National Study on Discrimination Against LGBTI Persons in Mexico: Right to Health by the CEAV and Fundación Arcoiris, an estimated 50 percent of the 3,451 respondents said "no," 18 percent said "occasionally," 6 percent said "frequently," and 3 percent said "always" when asked about derogatory or discriminatory comments from health care providers based on their sexual orientation or gender identity.104

[49] No doubt, the objective documentary evidence does state that the greatest challenge facing the LGBTQ community is in terms of their access to justice and security. According to one federal agency, crimes against sexual minorities is a constant phenomenon and is often motivated by social prejudice.105 Violence against sexual minorities and broad impunity for these crimes is a structural problem with the most affected being trans people, followed by gay men and lesbian women.106 According to a 2018 report on discrimination of LGBTQ people regarding access to justice and security by the CEAV and Fundación Arcoiris, an estimated 31 percent of transgender women respondents and approximately 15 percent of homosexuals said they had been detained because of their LGBTI status,107 during which many are subjected to mistreatment by the police.108 In its annual report on extreme violence against sexual minorities, the organization Letra S, AIDS, Culture and Daily Life indicates that more LGBT individuals were killed in 2017 and 2018 than in previous years (2013-2016), for reasons believed to be due to their real or perceived sexual or gender identity. The same source specifies that, from 2013 to 2018, 12 people from Yucatán were murdered.109 These are no doubt disturbing numbers and indicate that much remains to be done in terms of ensuring effective access to justice for the LGBTQ community. However, I do not find that these statistics and figures indicate that the discrimination the LGBTQ community faces, as indicative as they may be of ongoing discrimination, amounts to persecution.

[50] Moreover, NDP sources do indicate that there has been some progress. According to a representative from the Fundación Trans Amor progress has been made judicially, and that police bodies tend to follow the different protocols of action that have been issued by the federal government.110 Thus, while I do not belittle the allegations by the Principal Appellant that significant challenges remain, I find that the NDP-related sources paint a picture of mixed results and progress, and that based on the objective country documentation I am unable to find that the discrimination that the Principal Appellant may face if he returns to Mexico, in Mérida, for being a bisexual man (if analyzed cumulatively speaking) amounts to persecution.

[51] Specifically, with respect to Mérida, I take note of the information mentioned by the Principal Appellant that according to one NDP source, the treatment of sexual minorities varies from state to state and that Yucatán is one state where they are allegedly most ostracized.111 However, according to one source while the number of complaints of discrimination by police against sexual minorities was very high in some states, the list of these states did not include Yucatán.112 Other sources also indicate that the Yucatán State Human Rights Commission provides free legal services in cases of human rights abuses at a municipal or state level. In addition, there is Yucatrans, a collective of transgender people in Mérida that promotes the human rights of transgender and non-binary people. Furthermore, the Psychological, Sexological and Educational Attention Unit for Personal Growth (UNASSE), provides rapid HIV testing, a support group for HIV-positive clients and a free semi-structured support group for transgender persons every week. The source also states that in 2019, the mayor of Mérida, Yucatán announced the formation of the Municipal Council Against the Discrimination of Sexual Diversity, whose activities would include planning and evaluating activities aimed at fighting discrimination against sexual minorities.113

[52] Secondly, based on his personal evidence and testimony submitted by the Principal Appellant, I do not find that he has demonstrated a connection between the objective country documentation and his own particular circumstances, and vulnerabilities which would lead me to conclude that he faces a serious possibility of cumulative discrimination that amounts to persecution.114 In the PoE notes of the CBSA on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the Principal Appellant details his fear of returning to Nigeria. After the Officer denied the Appellant's entry into Canada, the Principal Appellant "stated that he and his family prefer to return to Mexico and that they will purchase their own tickets." According to these notes, the Principal Appellant then purchased tickets to Cancun Mexico for XXXX XXXX, 2019.115

[53] According to the PoE notes of the CBSA on XXXX XXXX, 2019, after purchasing the tickets, he was asked again whether he had any fear or problem of returning to Mexico to which he responded that he did not.116 When on XXXX XXXX, 2021, the Principal Appellant discloses to the CBSA officer that he wants to seek refugee protection, he stated that he used to be a bisexual man, but then stopped before getting married, but resumed a relationship with a Nigerian man he once knew in 2018. He also recounts why he fears returning to Nigeria, and that this has to do with Nigerian police authorities finding out that he is in a relationship with XXXX, The Principal Appellant also details his fear of returning to Mexico because he participated in a demonstration against the government in XXXX and that the police, that the police refused to offer protection and that a neighbor of the Appellants was shot and killed.117

[54] However, at no point does the Principal Appellant allege that he fears returning to Mexico because he would not be able to live his life openly as a bisexual man or that he fears persecution there because of his sexual orientation. Subsequently, in his written testimony attached to his BoC, the Appellant recounted the reasons why he fears returning to Mexico and Nigeria. With respect to Mexico, he only details his fear of returning there because of the SC and his participation in the protest. However, he makes no allegations that he fears returning there because of his bisexual orientation. I find that if he feared returning to Mexico because he fears persecution due to his sexual orientation as a bisexual man, the Principal Appellant would have made an effort to include it in his written testimony, even if previously, he had failed to mention it in his disclosure to the CBSA. Nor has he made any references to specific alleged acts of persecution or discrimination that may have taken place against him in Mexico in the past because of his sexual orientation.

[55] With respect to his personal circumstances, I do not find there is a serious possibility that he will face persecution, including serious physical violence, by reason of being a bisexual man when I take these circumstances into consideration. This is because although the Principal Appellant testified to having had a relationship with one other bisexual man in Mexico, he makes no mention anywhere in his oral or written testimony of having experienced any problems in Mexico for that reason. In addition, the Principal Appellant was able to frequent gay bars with his friend XXXX. I also do not find that the Principal Appellant has persuasively established that he was concealing his sexual orientation because he feared persecution from society at large. I find that evidence from his oral testimony, suggests that one reason is his children. During the RPD hearing, for example, the Principal Appellant alleged that he did not disclose his bisexual orientation to the CBSA officer when seeking refugee protection because the questioning was conducted before his children, and because he worried that "they will see me as not being very responsible if I had said other things in front of them."118 In addition, I note that the Principal Appellant would be relocating to Mérida with his wife and children, and does not allege that he seeks to separate from his wife and children there for the purpose of living together with another man or starting a family with another man as a same-sex couple.

[56] And while I am aware that persecution can be established by examining the treatment of similarly situated individuals and that an Appellant does not have to show that they have been persecuted in the past, 119 I find that when considering the context of the country conditions in Mexico with respect to LGBTQ individuals more generally, and the Principal Appellant's personal circumstances, of being still part of a family with wife and children, that if he relocates with them to Mérida, he would not be relocating to a place with a general atmosphere of insecurity, or one where the cumulative effects of the discrimination that he may face as a bisexual man, undermines his fundamental right in a manner that amounts to persecution.
3. Second Prong: Would it be objectively unreasonable for the Appellants, considering their personal circumstances, to relocate to Mérida?

[57] In his further submissions to the RAD, the Principal Appellant alleges that it would be objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Mérida because the Associate Appellant would be doing so as the breadwinner for the family without means of support; the Appellants have no family relatives at the proposed IFA locations; the Associate Appellant has no skills or work experience and minimal education; the Associate Appellant has language difficulties as she does not speak Spanish; the Associate Appellant is a visible minority in Mexico and that she has no recourse to social services because they are either lacking or inaccessible.

[58] The Associate Appellant would be relocating to Mérida with her husband, the Principal Appellant and her children. Nothing on the record before me, suggests that she would be moving there as the only or main family breadwinner. In addition, I point out that she is a Mexican national and has in the recent past already lived in Mexico for 8 years with her husband. Despite allegedly speaking little Spanish, and limited work experience, and finding it difficult at first to adapt, in her written narrative attached to her BoC, she testified that with time they loved Mexico and were slowly adapting to life in that country. If she and her family relocate to Mérida, I do not see that the challenges that she would face, would be significantly worse than what she encountered during her first efforts to reside in Mexico so as to render the conditions in that IFA objectively unreasonable. Here, I also underscore that according to the objective documentary evidence, 97.8 percent of the economically active population was employed; and that included 98.2 percent of the female population and 97.6 of the male population.120

[59] Determining that an IFA is unreasonable is a very high threshold, and requires "nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant".121 Under the second prong, the question is not whether the IFA is convenient or attractive to the Appellant, but whether it would be unduly harsh to expect him, in light of his personal circumstances, to move there before seeking refuge in Canada.122 And while the presence or absence of family in the IFA is a factor in assessing reasonableness, especially in the case of minor claimants, the absence of relatives in an IFA would have to jeopardize the safety of a claimant before that factor would make an IFA unreasonable. I do not find that the Associate Appellant has persuasively established that this would be the case. I also do not find that the Associate Appellant has provided sufficient evidence for her allegations that social services would be inaccessible or lacking in Mérida if the Appellants relocate there, particularly since all of the Appellants, including the children, are Mexican nationals. Nor do I find that she has credibly established that she would face difficulties because she is a visible minority to the extent that it would render the conditions in Mérida unreasonable. Finally, I do not find on the record before me any other allegations by the Principal Appellant of why the second prong of the IFA test would be met for him or the children if the Appellants relocate to Mérida.

[60] Given the above, I conclude that conditions in the proposed IFA location of Mérida are not objectively unreasonable, in all of the circumstances, including those particular to the Appellants for them to seek refuge there.
CONCLUSION

[61] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
